newsitem.title: JAPAN: Ford, GM may join U.S. firms in samurai bond drive.
newsitem.headline: Ford, GM may join U.S. firms in samurai bond drive.

text.p: General Motors Corp and Ford Motor Co are considering floating samurai bonds to Japanese investors, underwriting sources said on Tuesday, the latest in a string of such moves by U.S. corporations seeking lower funding costs.
An underwriting source at Nomura Securities said Ford is considering a yen/U.S. dollar dual-currency samurai by around early November.
Nomura, which would lead manage the issue, said the bond was likely to have a maturity of about three years and that the issue volume would be around 30 billion yen ($263 million).
Underwriting sources said General Motors Corp is also considering issuing dual-currency samurai bonds aimed at Japanese private investors.

Underwriters say the number of U.S. corporations seeking to raise funds in Japan by issuing samurai bonds has risen since Walt Disney Co launched 100 billion yen ($877 million) worth of dual currency samurais in late May. The samurais were lead managed by Nomura.
"Particularly after Walt Disney, we've been seeing many issues from U.S. corporations, and we expect this samurai issuing trend to continue," the source at Nomura said.
In the past couple of months, U.S. corporations including McDonald's Corp, International Business Machines Corp, and PepsiCo Inc have launched samurai issues.
"Companies like Walt Disney and McDonald's, which are familiar to many Japanese, have launched samurais before," said Masaru Hamazaki, deputy manager at Yamaichi Research Institute.
"The case should be same for Ford and GM. People know those names so it should be easier for them to raise funds through private investors in Japan," Hamazaki said.
The trend is not surprising given that debt issuers want to take advantage of rock-bottom Japanese interest rates while investors here are keen to avoid them.
Samurais are bonds denominated in yen issued by non-Japanese companies for sale mostly in Japan.

Underwriting sources estimate the volume of samurai bond issues from January to the end of October totalled 3.16 trillion yen ($27.7 billion). Of that, 1.79 trillion yen ($15.7 billion) were dual-currency issues.
"This move should get stronger as individuals become keener to diversify their funds into samurai or foreign bonds from domestic instruments," one senior underwriter said.

"In the past, people have not made a profit out of foreign bond investment, but the recent depreciation of the yen has made it possible to receive higher returns from foreign bond investments," he added.
But private investors might become more careful about buying bonds in foreign currencies, some market sources said, since a reversal in the yen's fall could wipe out their profits.

"It's time for private investors to start taking a more careful stance towards dual-currency samurai investment," Hamazaki said. "It seems that the excessive samurai issuing trend is slowly peaking out due to increasing speculation that the fall of the yen will be limited." ($1=114 yen)
